failure_modes.description: Local reward signals cannot accurately reflect system performance in complex traffic networks
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems are inherently non-linear and emergent; local improvements often create bottlenecks elsewhere (Braess paradox)

failure_modes.description: Distributed reinforcement learning cannot effectively manage the exploration-exploitation balance in large-scale traffic systems
failure_modes.evidence: Multi-agent RL suffers from non-stationarity problems where the environment changes as other agents learn, making stable convergence nearly impossible

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis ignores critical boundary conditions of real-world traffic systems
failure_modes.evidence: Emergency vehicles, weather events, accidents, and construction zones create extreme conditions that break the learning assumptions

failure_modes.description: Numerous existing distributed traffic control systems already outperform RL approaches
failure_modes.evidence: SCATS, SCOOT, and RHODES systems have decades of proven performance in real cities with predictable, optimized timing

failure_modes.description: The system would catastrophically fail during peak hours when exploration is most dangerous
failure_modes.evidence: Exploration requires random timing changes that would cause gridlock during high traffic periods

failure_modes.description: Traffic optimization objectives are fundamentally incompatible with pure reward maximization
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems require multi-objective optimization (throughput, safety, emissions, equity) that cannot be reduced to a single reward signal
